message:
Pool bignum's two per-value heap allocations

Every bignum construction cost two separate heap allocations: the
handle's own malloc in bignum_new, plus GMP's internal digit-buffer
malloc inside mpf_init2 -- both hit the system allocator fresh every
time, even though the exact same size gets requested and freed
constantly at any given precision.

Profiled standalone before implementing, against a theoretical floor
(no allocation at all, just reusing one persistent handle), not just a
before/after: pooling landed within ~1-2x of that floor, ~5-8x faster
than plain malloc/free -- the biggest win found this session, well
past the smaller targeted fixes (chain fusion, literal hoisting,
tetration's loop) that came before it.

Added a size-bucketed freelist pool to runtime/gmp/bignum_shim.c.
Buckets are found by a linear scan keyed on requested size -- fine
since the number of distinct sizes a program uses is small (bounded by
how many different precisions appear in the source, not by how many
bignums are ever constructed). mp_set_memory_functions redirects GMP's
own internal allocations through the pool; bignum_new/bignum_free's own
wrapper allocation routes through the identical pool functions
directly. Installed via __attribute__((constructor)) so it's in effect
before the very first bignum_new, with zero codegen changes needed.
Unsynchronized (no locks) since CyborgPL programs are single-threaded.

Verified: ~2.5x on a real end-to-end workload (function calls +
arithmetic dilute the pure-allocation win, as expected). Multiple
simultaneous precisions land in separate buckets with no cross-
corruption (a 64-bit and a 1000-bit accumulator in the same loop both
produced exactly correct values). No unbounded growth -- peak memory
footprint was flat between 50 and 2,000,000 repeated allocations at
the same size. Full example-suite regression pass, plus every bignum
test file from this session's earlier rounds re-confirmed correct.

One real, deliberate tradeoff: a pooled block is never returned to the
OS once freed, only kept for reuse -- a program with a brief burst of
many live bignums, then very few, keeps that memory reserved for the
rest of the run.
